rewritten_text:
Smallpox!

I rushed to the king and whispered in his ear:

“Get out at once, sire! This woman is dying of the disease that devastated the outskirts of Camelot two years ago.”

He did not move.

“I will stay, and I will help.”

I whispered again:

“King, you cannot stay. You must leave.”

“You mean well, and your advice is sensible. But a king should be ashamed to show fear, and a knight should be ashamed to refuse help to people in need. Enough. I will not leave. You are the one who must go. The Church’s ban does not apply to me, but it forbids you to be here. If the Church hears you have disobeyed, it will punish you severely.”

He was in terrible danger, and staying might cost him his life, but arguing was useless. Once he believed his honor as a knight was involved, there was nothing more to discuss. He would stay, and nothing could stop him. I knew that, so I let the matter drop. The woman spoke:

“Kind sir, will you please climb that ladder and tell me what you find? Do not be afraid to speak. There are times when even a mother’s heart can no longer break, because it is already broken.”

“Stay here,” said the king, “and give her something to eat. I will go.” He set down the knapsack.

I turned to go, but he was already moving. He stopped and looked down at a man lying in the faint light, who had neither noticed us nor spoken.

“Is this your husband?” the king asked.

“Yes.”

“Is he asleep?”

“Thank God for that one mercy, yes—for three hours now. How can I ever give enough thanks? My heart is bursting with gratitude for the sleep he is enjoying.”

I said:

“We will be careful not to wake him.”

“Ah, no, you will not. He is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes, and what a victory it is to know that! No one can hurt him or insult him again. He is happy in heaven now. Or, if he is not there, he is content in hell, for he will find neither abbot nor bishop there. We grew up together, a boy and a girl. We were husband and wife for twenty-five years, never parted until today. Think how long that is to love and suffer together. This morning his mind wandered. He imagined we were children again, walking through the happy fields. Talking with innocent delight, he wandered farther and farther, still chatting cheerfully, until he entered those other fields we know nothing of and passed beyond mortal sight.

“The bewilderment and astonishment this extraordinary change in circumstances produced in me may, after all, be the least explicable part of the adventure. The reversal itself was both natural and inevitable. I had, in fact, long expected it to occur at precisely that stage of my journey when the planet’s attraction would be overcome by that of its satellite—or, more accurately, when the balloon’s gravitational pull toward the earth became weaker than its pull toward the moon. Admittedly, I had awakened from a deep sleep, my senses thoroughly confused, to confront a startling phenomenon which, though anticipated, I had not expected at that particular moment. The actual rotation must, of course, have happened smoothly and gradually. It is by no means certain that, even had I been awake while it occurred, I would have detected any internal sign of the inversion—that is, any discomfort or disturbance affecting either my body or my equipment.

“It scarcely needs saying that, once I properly understood my position and recovered from the terror that had overwhelmed every faculty of my mind, I first devoted my entire attention to studying the moon’s general physical appearance. It spread beneath me like a map. Although I estimated that it remained a considerable distance away, the irregularities of its surface were visible with a striking, utterly inexplicable clarity. At first sight, the most extraordinary geological feature was its complete lack of oceans or seas—indeed, of any lake, river, or other body of water. Strangely, however, I could see vast flat regions whose character was unmistakably that of land formed by waterborne sediment. Most of the visible hemisphere, though, was covered by countless conical volcanic mountains, which looked more like artificial constructions than natural elevations. The tallest rises no more than three and three-quarter miles vertically. A map of the volcanic areas of the Campi Phlegraei would give your Excellencies a better impression of their overall surface than any inadequate description I might attempt. Most were plainly erupting, and they made me terrifyingly aware of their violence and power through the repeated thunder of the stones mistakenly called meteoric, which now shot upward past the balloon with increasingly alarming frequency.

We spent a few sorrowful hours waiting for eleven o’clock, when the trial was due to begin. My father and the rest of the family had to attend as witnesses, so I went with them to court. Throughout that miserable mockery of justice I endured terrible torment. The court would decide whether my curiosity and reckless experiments would lead to the deaths of two people. One was a smiling child, full of innocence and happiness. The other would suffer an even more dreadful murder, made more horrifying by the shame attached to it. Justine was a good young woman whose qualities should have brought her a happy life. Now all that promise was to end in a dishonored grave—and I was responsible! A thousand times over, I would rather have confessed to the crime she was accused of. But I had been elsewhere when it happened. Such a confession would have been dismissed as a madman’s ravings and would not have cleared the woman suffering because of me.

Justine appeared calm. She wore mourning clothes, and the seriousness of her feelings made her face, always attractive, extraordinarily beautiful. She seemed secure in her innocence and did not tremble, though thousands stared at her and cursed her. Whatever kindness her beauty might otherwise have stirred had been driven from their minds by thoughts of the terrible crime they believed she had committed. She was composed, but clearly maintaining that composure took effort. Since her earlier confusion had been used as evidence of guilt, she forced herself to look brave. On entering the court she glanced around and quickly found where we were sitting. A tear seemed to cloud her eye when she saw us, but she immediately regained control. Her expression of sorrowful affection seemed to declare her complete innocence.

The trial opened. After the lawyer prosecuting her had explained the charge, several witnesses were called. A number of strange facts worked against her. They might have shaken anyone who lacked the proof of her innocence that I possessed. She had been away from home all night when the murder took place. Near morning, a woman going to market had seen her close to where the murdered child’s body was later discovered. The woman asked what she was doing there. Justine looked very strange and gave only a confused answer that made no sense. She came home around eight o’clock. When someone asked where she had spent the night, she said she had been searching for the child and urgently asked whether anyone had heard anything about him.
